explain.say: Two tramps wait by a bare tree on a country road for someone called Godot. He never comes. Samuel Beckett's play opened in Paris in 1953, in French, and one Irish critic joked that nothing happens in it, and it happens twice. The board puts the two acts side by side. Can you spot the differences?

explain.say: Here are the characters, in pairs. Vladimir thinks and remembers; Estragon struggles with his boots and forgets. Then Pozzo arrives, driving his servant Lucky on a rope like an animal. Each evening a boy brings word that Godot will come tomorrow. Which pair feels like a friendship, and which like power?

explain.say: Why absurd? In 1961 the critic Martin Esslin called plays like this the Theatre of the Absurd: they show people searching for meaning in a universe that offers none. Look at the reasons: a Europe wrecked by war, Albert Camus's image of Sisyphus pushing his rock uphill for ever, and talk that circles. Is waiting the same as hoping?

explain.say: Now the second act. The tree has sprouted a few leaves, Pozzo has gone blind and Lucky mute, and the boy says the same thing. Each act ends with the two men agreeing to leave, and not moving. The repetition is not lazy; it is the point. What has changed, and what has not?

explain.say: The play travelled far. In 1957 it was performed in San Quentin prison in California, and many prisoners understood it at once: they knew all about waiting. When asked who Godot was, Beckett replied, in effect, that he did not know, or he would have put it in the play. Brilliant. Challenge: stage two minutes of waiting with no words.

faq.a: The play never says. Some see God, others death, hope, meaning or simply someone who will not come. Beckett refused to explain, saying in effect that if he knew he would have put it in the play.

faq.q: What is the Theatre of the Absurd?
faq.a: A label from Martin Esslin's 1961 book for post-war plays by Beckett, Ionesco, Genet and others that show human beings seeking meaning in a purposeless world, using circular plots and broken dialogue.

faq.q: Why does nothing happen in Waiting for Godot?
faq.a: Beckett makes waiting itself the action. The repetition of the two acts shows time passing without progress, inviting the audience to feel the boredom, hope and companionship of waiting.

faq.q: What do Pozzo and Lucky represent?
faq.a: Readings include master and slave, capitalist and worker, or body and mind. Pozzo controls Lucky with a rope, but in Act Two the blind Pozzo depends on him, so power itself looks absurd.

faq.q: Why did prisoners love Waiting for Godot?
faq.a: When the San Francisco Actor's Workshop played it in San Quentin prison in 1957, inmates recognised its endless waiting and uncertain release from their own lives, and responded far more warmly than many critics had.

facts: Waiting for Godot premiered on 5 January 1953 at the Théâtre de Babylone in Paris.
Beckett wrote it first in French and translated it into English himself.
Beckett won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1969.
